newsitem.title: USA: Away on Business: The Taxed Traveler.
newsitem.headline: Away on Business: The Taxed Traveler.

text.p: Business travelers will shell out millions of dollars in travel taxes in the coming year in a soak-the-moving-target trend that shows no signs of abating.
That view comes from the Travel Industry Association of America which reports that governments continue to pile up taxes on hotel guests, gasoline, airport use, dining out and car rentals.
There are 17 cities alone, it says, that have or would like to impose taxes to pay for new sports stadiums or arenas.

"These taxes are all continuing to rise," said Shawn Flaherty, spokeswoman for the association. "Travelers are increasingly becoming targets because they have no retribution in terms of voting someone out of office."
Cities that tax travelers heavily may eventually suffer some loss of business, she added, but that is slow in coming and hard to measure.

The national average tax levy is $3 for airport facility use, 40 cents a gallon for gasoline, 7.2 percent for restaurant food, 12 percent for hotel rooms and 8.2 percent plus a surcharge for car rentals.
On the last, the taxes tend to be slightly lower if the car is rented from a location away from the airport.

-- The Washington-based Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine says the healthiest airport food among 25 airports it surveyed can be found at Los Angeles International. The criteria used were the availability of low-fat and vegetarian dishes.

The other airports in the top 10 in order were Vancouver, Detroit, Minneapolis-St. Paul, Seattle-Tacoma, Pittsburgh, Dallas, Phoenix, Chicago and Salt Lake City. Last place went to Cleveland's Hopkins.
-- Travelers grabbing a gift en route to the plane most often choose a regional food speciality or related gift basket, according to Host Marriott Services which operates shops at many airports.
Coffee gift sets are the second most popular item.

-- The move to provide plug-in power supply for laptop computer users on the move is expanding. At-the-seat power supplies are slowly working their way into some airliners on an experimental basis and may soon be available on some trains.
Amtrak recently unveiled a revamped Metroliner for its East Coast service which features a plug at each seat.
